reports.name: Elly De La Cruz
reports.published_report: The contact quality is about as loud as it gets: 94.7 mph average exit velocity ranks at the 99th percentile, and a 16.4% barrel rate sits at the 98th. The tension in the profile is that all that raw violence against the ball is still being filtered through a 27.7% strikeout rate, which is a real drag on how often it shows up in the box score. The .374 xwOBA and .504 xSLG say the underlying skill is genuine and the projection's .282/.359/.511 line with 29 home runs and 28 stolen bases is what he looks like when the strikeouts stay manageable — which they have been trending toward, given 10.6% walk rate keeping him in counts. If the whiff rate stops improving, you're left with a boom-or-bust middle-of-the-order bat who still provides elite run-scoring value on the bases; if the zone discipline keeps tightening, you're looking at a true five-category cornerstone.

reports.name: Sal Stewart
reports.published_report: The xSLG sits at .475 with a 12.7% barrel rate, and together they tell you the power is doing real work in contact quality. What makes the profile interesting is that the barrel frequency is genuinely elite while the hard-hit rate at 40.1% sits right around league average, which means he's squaring up a smaller, more precise slice of contact rather than mashing everything indiscriminately. The xwOBA of .348 runs well ahead of the .258 xBA, so the value is concentrated in the extra-base events, and the projection's .472 SLG across 702 PA is a reasonable translation of that shape. If the 27.3% whiff rate creeps up against premium stuff, this becomes a corner bat leaning on the power to carry the line, but at 22, the barrel rate gives him room to work with.

reports.name: Bobby Witt Jr.

That's the tension: elite batted-ball profile, genuine swing-and-miss-outside-the-zone problem dragging the surface line down toward merely very good. The 43 projected steals at 30.1 ft/s sprint speed add a dimension most hitters with this kind of exit-velo profile don't carry. If the chase rate tightens even modestly, the .510 xSLG starts showing up in the actual slash line and this becomes an MVP conversation; if it doesn't, you still have an everyday shortstop posting an .811 OPS with stolen-base volume that keeps him top-of-lineup relevant.

If the control holds, you're looking at a genuine ace.

reports.name: Kade Anderson
reports.published_report: A 1.1 ERA and a 0.6 WHIP at Double-A aren't numbers that need context — they're the argument. Anderson has struck out 135 batters against 13 walks across 93.3 innings at AA this season, and the command profile translates cleanly: a BB/9 of 2.0 in MLB terms, well below the 3.2 figure where most pitchers land, with a K-BB% that comes out to 21.9% against an average of 13.5%. The whole thing hinges on whether the stuff backs up the control at the highest level, because a left-hander this young who misses this many bats while almost never missing the zone has no obvious developmental ceiling short of a frontline starter. If the stuff softens in the jump, he's still a useful mid-rotation arm, but nothing in this line suggests you should expect softening.

reports.name: Corbin Carroll
reports.published_report: The contact rates are the only thing keeping this from being a clearcut star profile. Carroll's exit velocity grades at the 88th percentile, his sprint speed at 29.7 ft/s sits at the 97th percentile, and an 11.0% walk rate gives him a disciplined foundation — yet a 27.8% whiff rate drags his xBA down to .249 while his xSLG and xwOBA (.448 and .343) tell a meaningfully better power story. The gap between those two clusters is the whole profile: he makes hard contact when he connects, he runs as well as almost anyone in the league, but he misses enough to suppress the batting average and keep the upside from fully surfacing in the box score. If the whiff rate comes down even modestly, the .332 OBP and .471 projected SLG start to feel conservative; if it stays where it is, he's a 23-homer, 23-steal contributor whose counting stats carry the value more than the rates do.

reports.name: Carter Jensen
reports.published_report: The power contact profile here is genuinely miserable at the same time it's impressive. Jensen's 91.4 mph average exit velocity sits in the 84th percentile, his 12.2% barrel rate in the 78th, and yet his xBA is .217, because a 29.4% whiff rate is quietly eating the entire foundation. The contact that lands is loud; the contact that doesn't exist is the problem. If the strikeout rate, currently 28.1%, doesn't come down as he accumulates major-league at-bats, the projection's .232 AVG becomes optimistic and the 26 home runs stay out of reach behind a parade of empty at-bats, but if he can tighten the zone even modestly, his 24.1% chase rate already grades favorably, and there's a genuine middle-of-the-order catching profile here rather than a streaky power bat buried in the eight-hole.

reports.name: Zack Gelof
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile here is pulling in two directions at once. Gelof makes hard contact, a 9.5% barrel rate and 42.4% hard-hit, but a 29.1% whiff rate drags the xBA down to .230 and keeps the xwOBA at a middling .313. The 24.9% chase rate is legitimately good, so this isn't a guy flailing at slop outside the zone; he's getting to strikes and still missing them at an uncomfortable clip, and until that changes the power-over-average profile has a ceiling. If the contact rate firms up even modestly, the underlying exit quality translates to something closer to the projected .457 SLG; if it doesn't, the .251/.317 line is roughly what you're getting, a second-division regular with 20 home runs, real speed at 28.8 ft/s, and a swing-and-miss problem that keeps him from the next tier.

The xBA of .259 is believable given the contact skill, but an xwOBA of .286 and xSLG of .326 are hard to dress up — there's almost no thump behind the bat. What carries the profile is the 29.5 ft/s sprint speed, which is genuine elite-tier and shows up in the projection's 17 stolen bases, giving him a path to run value that his bat alone wouldn't earn. If the chase rate tightens and he learns to work counts, this becomes a legitimate table-setter; if it doesn't, .315 OBP is probably the ceiling on a below-average offensive profile, and he's a fourth outfielder who runs really, really well.

reports.name: Jakob Marsee
reports.published_report: The OBP is the whole argument. Marsee's 12.7% walk rate sits in the 89th percentile, his chase rate is in the 91st, and those two numbers together explain how a hitter with an xSLG at the 7th percentile can project to a .341 on-base mark across 619 plate appearances. The bat-to-ball quality is genuinely thin, 87.4 mph average exit velocity and a 3.5% barrel rate, so what he offers is zone discipline and 24 projected steals, not damage. If the walks dry up even a little, there's not enough slug behind them to carry a lineup spot, and a .226/.341/.351 line already asks you to accept him purely on on-base and speed value; the fielding grades at the 94th percentile give him a real second argument, but that's a defense-first, bat-last profile that lands him as a useful regular rather than an everyday centerpiece.

reports.name: Jett Williams

The whole profile hinges on whether the batting average, currently sitting at .233 AAA with a .282 BABIP, can stabilize enough at the big-league level to keep the OBP functional without the power to compensate when it doesn't. Either a fringy everyday regular if the contact improves, or a bench bat whose walks keep him employed.

Cam Cannarella is hitting .330 across AAA & AA & A+ with 59 walks against 76 strikeouts in 418 plate appearances, a contact-and-patience combination that ranks at the 99th and 98th percentile in OBP and average within the hitter pool, but the MLB translation cools the ISO to .148, sitting right where league average sits, and puts the strikeout rate near 20.9% in a league where the number to beat is 22.0. The walk rate survives better, translating to 11.3%, which is a useful edge over the 8.5% baseline. The whole profile hinges on whether the average holds even partially, because if the .330 bleeds down to something ordinary, the power isn't there to carry him, and what's left is a plate-discipline profile with no carrying tool. He's either a useful table-setter if the bat-to-ball skill translates, or a bench piece with a pretty minor-league line.

reports.name: Max Anderson
reports.published_report: The contact is the whole argument. Across AAA & A in 2026, Max Anderson has struck out just 65 times in 473 plate appearances, a 14% rate that translates to 17.1% against big-league pitching while the MLB average sits at 22.0%. That same contact quality pushes his .300 average and .385 OBP into territory that makes you want to keep going, and his 53 walks show the zone awareness is genuine discipline rather than passive at-bats. The ceiling hinges entirely on whether his .149 MLB-equivalent ISO can grow beyond essentially league-mean power, because if it stays flat, you have a high-contact second baseman whose floor and ceiling are closer together than you'd like: a useful bench bat, maybe a platoon piece if a team likes the contact profile enough to build around it.

reports.name: Cody Bellinger
reports.published_report: The contact grades carry this profile. Bellinger's xBA sits at .273 (84th percentile) while his K% of 15.7% lands in the 82nd percentile, and those two numbers tell you what he actually is right now: a disciplined, bat-to-ball outfielder who makes the game look quieter than his peak suggested. The power hasn't followed, with a 6.6% barrel rate and 37.6% hard-hit rate both sitting in the bottom third of the league, and the .414 xSLG bears that out. reports.name: Nathan Flewelling

Everything here hinges on whether the strikeout rate bends as he climbs; if it doesn't, what's left is a bench catcher with acceptable plate discipline and middling pop.

He's a solid everyday outfielder whose value lives entirely in the walk and the glove.

At AA, 21 walks across 126 innings translates to a 2.1 BB/9 in MLB-equivalent terms, well below the 3.2 mark most pitchers run at that level, and that gap is wide enough to carry a guy whose 99 strikeouts don't translate to missing bats up top — the MLB-equivalent K/9 comes out at 6.6, well short of the 8.6 average. The control is real enough to keep him viable, but the ceiling math doesn't clear the bar: even with pinpoint command, a pitcher who misses few bats and works toward the middle of the zone doesn't have the margin for error a backend starter needs. Suarez is a depth arm if it stays together, and a depth arm if something slips.

reports.name: Jared Jones
reports.published_report: The fastball sits at 98.3 mph and spins at 2541 rpm, and that combination is what makes a 32.6% whiff rate believable across a real MLB sample. Jones gets hitters to swing and miss at an elite clip, but the walk rate at 8.4% is exactly league average, and that's the tension: the stuff earns strikeouts at a 28.0% clip while the command does nothing to help. His xERA of 3.42 and xwOBA of .287 say the underlying quality is meaningfully better than a 4.03 projected ERA, and if the walks tighten even modestly, the gap between what he is and what the run-prevention numbers show closes fast. The version where the walks stay put is still a useful mid-rotation arm; the version where he finds the zone more consistently is something Pittsburgh hasn't seen in a while.

reports.name: Alexander Cornielle
reports.published_report: The ERA is eye-catching and the walk rate is the reason to worry. Across AAA, AA & A in 2026, Cornielle has posted a 2.70 ERA over 77 innings, but that WHIP of 1.3 and a 4.7 BB/9 point to a pitcher living dangerously, and when you translate the control to MLB context, the 4.3 BB/9 sits well above a league average closer to 3.2. His strikeout rate translates to 8.2 per nine at the MLB level, essentially average, which means the walk rate isn't being masked by swing-and-miss the way a true power arm might get away with it. Everything here hinges on whether he tightens the zone: if he does, there's a backend starter or swingable reliever in there; if he doesn't, the stuff isn't loud enough to carry the free passes and he lands as a depth arm.

reports.name: Logan Webb
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile here is a riddle: a 6.1% walk rate that grades well above most starters, a 5.8% barrel rate that says hitters aren't doing damage when they connect, and yet a 20.1% strikeout rate that ranks below two-thirds of the league. Webb survives on contact management rather than swing-and-miss, and the 21.5% whiff rate confirms there isn't a hidden chase-and-miss weapon waiting to surface. The whole profile holds together only if he keeps inducing weak, early contact — the 32.9% chase rate helps, but with that fastball sitting 92.3 mph with bottom-two-percent spin, he has almost no margin if hitters start waiting him out. A 4.08 xERA says the run-prevention is roughly what a league-average arm would produce, and the projected 4.26 ERA across 174.0 innings lands right there: a durable, back-of-rotation piece who eats innings without getting shelled, but whose ceiling is capped by the strikeout floor.

reports.name: Axiel Plaz
reports.published_report: The A+ line is genuinely pretty — .305/.389/.513 through 412 plate appearances, with 18 home runs and a 10% walk rate sitting comfortably alongside a 17% strikeout rate. At the catcher position, that contact-and-patience combination is unusual enough to notice. But the MLB translation is where the ceiling conversation gets complicated: A+ power at .207 ISO softens to .144 at the big-league level, landing just below a league-average mark of .150, and the walk rate follows a similar path downward. If the bat speed and recognition that produce those A+ results translate cleanly, a real question across two to three years and several levels, you get a functional big-league catcher with a serviceable floor; if the hit tool fades when pitching gets sharper, what's left is organizational depth behind the plate.

reports.name: Peter Lambert
reports.published_report: The xERA of 3.69 is the honest number here — not the strikeout rate, which sits at a middling 22.9%, and not the fastball, which at 93.9 mph doesn't beat anyone on its own. What Lambert does is keep the ball off the barrel: a 6.4% barrel rate and 35.8% hard-hit rate that together paint a contact manager who gets weak enough contact to survive without a dominant swing-and-miss pitch. The 9.1% walk rate is the fragile piece, because a guy living on soft contact can't also be putting runners on for free. If the walks tighten, he profiles as a durable mid-rotation arm eating deep into games in Houston; if they don't, the whole thing compresses into a swingman with a flattering ERA.

reports.name: Conor Essenburg
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the loudest thing in this profile, and it's also the thing that keeps the ceiling conversation short. Across A+ & A in 415 plate appearances, Essenburg has drawn 83 walks against 120 strikeouts, a 20% walk rate that translates to roughly 13.5% at the MLB level, while the power (17 home runs, .239 ISO) melts to a .148 MLB-equivalent, indistinguishable from a typical big leaguer. The discipline is genuine and rare for a 19-year-old; the problem is that a 32.9% translated strikeout rate attached to average-equivalent power is a profile built for depth rather than impact, and if the contact doesn't develop as he climbs, the walks become the whole argument for a roster spot. Either a patient bench bat who earns playing time with his on-base ability, or a fringe name if the strikeouts harden against better stuff.

At 19 years old, 41 stolen bases in 553 plate appearances make the speed case clearly — that part doesn't need a translator. What does need one is the bat: the MLB-equivalent K% comes out to 24.6, a tick above where MLB hitters sit, and the translated ISO lands at .108 when the MLB average is .15, meaning the present pop doesn't carry. The .37 BABIP is doing real work behind that .305, and a center fielder who runs like this can sustain some BABIP lift, but the walk rate at 7% translates to 6.4, and that's a thin margin for contact-driven profiles when the strikeouts tick up. If the speed plays in center and the hit tool matures, there's a second-division regular in here; if the contact rate stalls and the BABIP regresses, what's left is a bench outfielder who can run.

The contact isn't there yet, a .224 average with a .248 BABIP suggests the hit tool is genuinely thin, and the raw power translates to a .144 ISO at the MLB level, right around average rather than a carrying tool. reports.name: Mason Peters
reports.published_report: The 2.1 ERA across A+ & A is the loud number, but what makes it worth taking seriously is the shape behind it: 87 strikeouts in 64.3 innings with only 19 walks, a 0.9 WHIP, a K-BB% of 27 that ranks at the 98th percentile in his pool. Strip that down to what it translates to at the MLB level and it deflates quickly — the strikeout rate comes out to 8.4 per nine, essentially matching what an average major-league arm produces, and the walk rate lands in the same neighborhood, so the margins that look dominant in A-ball basically become a league-average pitcher. That's the whole profile: the stuff plays up in the lower minors, and if it doesn't add a genuine swing-and-miss weapon as he climbs, the floor is a depth arm with no real ceiling to argue over.

reports.published_report: The contact and patience are genuinely loud: a .424 OBP and 80 walks across AAA & AA & A+ with only 57 strikeouts in 509 plate appearances, and the MLB translation puts his K% at 15.6 against a league-wide 22.0. Pitre puts the ball in play and takes his walks at rates that would play in the big leagues tomorrow. The problem is everything else — an .107 MLB-equivalent ISO tells you the bat doesn't scare anyone, and 35 stolen bases can paper over a lot of slugging until they can't. If the power never develops past what it is now, you're looking at a bench bat who earns walks and doesn't hurt you, not a regular.
reports.report: The sample covers 509 PA in Triple-A, Double-A, and High-A, so confidence is high. He consistently finishes at-bats with contact. Pitchers have little reason to avoid the zone. Contact-first table-setter shape, with present damage that still looks reserve-level.
